newsitem.title: UK: Non-OPEC Q2 supply up for first time in years - IE.
newsitem.headline: Non-OPEC Q2 supply up for first time in years - IE.

text.p: Non-OPEC oil supply in the second quarter of 1997 is expected to show a modest increase over the first quarter, bucking a five year quarter-to-quarter pattern of declining or steady output, the International Energy Agency said.

New start-ups, repairs and upgrades to North Sea fields and accelerating Latin American production growth should more than compensate for maintenance outages, lifting non-OPEC supply by 100,000 barrels per day (bpd).

"Last year, relatively light North Sea maintenance and increases in non-OECD supply resulted in a flat quarter-to-quarter pattern versus an average (decline) of around 0.5 million bpd in the previous four years," the IEA said.

The biggest regional non-OPEC supply increase in the second quarter should come from Latin America, adding 150,000 bpd to its first quarter total thanks to new fields in Mexico, lighter maintenance in Brazil's Campos Basin, repairs to the main Ecuadorian pipeline and seasonal increases in Argentina.
Non-OPEC Latin American supply should rise by 460,000 barrels bpd in 1997, with Brazil, Mexico and Colombia accounting for more than 75 percent of the increase, the Paris-based agency said.

North Sea production will rise by 134,000 bpd in the second quarter, largely due to the addition of seven new fields in British waters, and the growth will continue into the third quarter, the IEA said.

"The total North Sea net maintenance impact is expected to be around 100,000 bpd in the third quarter 1997 versus over 250,000 bpd in combined new field additions and repairs and upgrades, resulting in a net increase of almost 110,000 bpd," the agency said in its latest monthly oil market report.
World oil demand is expected to decline by 2.4 million bpd from the first quarter to the second, 600,000 bpd lower than the five-year average and 900,000 bpd lower than the equivalent fall in 1996.
More than 80 percent of the decline is expected to take place in OECD countries, the IEA said.
"The seasonal decline in OECD demand is less than the average experienced in the 1990s, primarily due to significantly milder weather in the first quarter 1997 than a year earlier," it said.
The IEA revised down its world oil demand estimate for the first quarter by 400,000 bpd to 74.2 million bpd.
